newsitem.title: UK: Western traders head to Iraq to arrange oil export.
newsitem.headline: Western traders head to Iraq to arrange oil export.

text.p: Western oil traders on Monday were planning to visit Iraq to sign the first crude export contracts since 1990 as key players expressed satisfaction with the prices set by Baghdad last week, industry sources said.
"They're fine, they'll work," said a trader for U.S. independent refiner Coastal Corp in response to news of the prices. He said he would be travelling to Baghdad later this week.
Last month, Iraq accepted U.N. terms for the partial flow of crude oil to world markets after a six-year blockade under an embargo imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The deal signed in May provides for limited exports worth $2 billion every six months to enable Baghdad to buy food and medicine.
Iraq's state oil firm SOMO last week set the price of Kirkuk Blend crude for December loading to European customers at a discount of $1.55 a barrel to benchmark Dated Brent quotations.
For customers in the U.S., Kirkuk will be priced at a discount of $3.00 to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude.
Houston-based Coastal is expected to lift the lion's share of Iraqi crude exports, which should amount to 500-550,000 barrels per day (bpd) at today's prices.
Prior to the Gulf crisis, Coastal lifted about 10 percent of Iraqi exports, or about 225,000 bpd, for its refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
Some European traders said they received a faxed invitation to Baghdad from Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) last Thursday, while others were still waiting for an approach.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf was quoted in Baghdad newspapers as saying on Monday that Iraq had already started striking deals with foreign firms for the sale of crude under the oil-for food deal with the United Nations.
"As soon as we get something in writing we're going over there," said a dealer for a U.K.-based trading house active in the Mediterranean sour crude market.
The trader said that the December price for Kirkuk export grade of Dated Brent less $1.55 a barrel fob Ceyhan looked attractive relative to alternative sour crudes such as Russian Urals.
"At this minute it's attractive," he said.

But this trader and others said that Iraqi crude could lose some of its appeal when flows start to loosen up the tight Mediterranean sour crude market which currently prices Urals as high as parity to Dated Brent on a delivered basis.
"As soon as (Iraqi crude) comes out it won't look so good...Urals will go down," he said.
Term contracts will run for three months with the price tied to Arab Light crude, which some traders believe is slow to respond to market fundamentals.
"The price could move 10 or 20 cents up or down, but it won't be that market-responsive," the trader said.
Other traders and refiners were concerned that SOMO had set the Kirkuk price too high.
"I don't think many people will lift at these prices but they won't have any trouble placing the oil," said one.
A trader for a Belgian refiner said he was still studying the economics of lifting Iraqi crude.
"We have not yet made a decision whether to sign or not," he said. "We think the price is a little bit too high, maybe 20 cents."
An Italian refiner was also cautious.
"I'd say the price in the Med is a bit high. I cannot say whether we're going to sign an agreement or not, it's delicate."
-- Rosalind Russell, Mark Thompson, London +44 171 542 5387
